somalia.title: Attorney General Rejects Supreme Court Ruling as "Lacking Legal Basis" in Deepening Constitutional Standoff - Somali News today Live - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Attorney General Rejects Supreme Court Ruling as "Lacking Legal Basis" in Deepening Constitutional Standoff - Somali News today Live MOGADISHU , Somalia’s Attorney General has formally rejected the Supreme Court’s ruling on the constitutional case and the Chief Justice’s dismissal, declaring the court’s decision “lacking any legal basis” and vowing to take “appropriate legal action,” in a move that deepens the constitutional standoff between the executive and the judiciary. In a statement issued on November 6, the Office of the Attorney General said it had submitted legal objections to the Supreme Court regarding the court’s jurisdiction and the legal standing of the petitioner, former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed. It accused the judges of violating procedural rules, failing to respond to its objections, and “creating a new case” that was not the one originally filed. As FTL Somalia reported when the Attorney General first demanded amendment records , the government had been preparing its legal defense since October, requesting documentation from both houses of parliament and the Justice Ministry ahead of its scheduled response to the court. The Attorney General’s intervention came a day after the Supreme Court issued a sweeping ruling that declared the mandates of the President, Parliament, and the Federal Government expired in 2026, and ordered elections within 90 days. The court had also declared President Mohamud’s dismissal of Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed “null and void” and accused the presidency of attempting to obstruct the constitutional case, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the constitutional standoff . The Attorney General’s Objections The Attorney General’s statement laid out a series of procedural complaints against the court. It argued that the court should have first ruled on the government’s legal objections before issuing a judgment, and that it violated the principle of adversarial proceedings by not allowing both sides to be heard. It further accused the court of violating its own structural rules, alleging that the Chief Justice should have presided over the panel of judges hearing the case, and that the court “created a new case” by ruling on matters that were not part of the original petition. The statement concluded that the court’s ruling “does not serve the national interest or the completion of the building of the Somali state” and therefore “has no legal effect.” The Attorney General’s Office said it would “take the appropriate legal step.” A Standoff With No Clear Resolution The Attorney General’s rejection of the ruling marks the latest escalation in a confrontation that has moved from the courtroom to the streets. On Thursday, Somali government troops deployed in large numbers around the Supreme Court, and Chief Justice Baashe was ordered to leave the premises, according to a senior judge who spoke to BBC Somali. The court’s official Facebook page, which had been used to publish recent rulings, was also taken offline. The allegation was first raised publicly by opposition presidential candidate Abdirahman Abdishakur Warsame, who accused the President of deploying troops to arrest the Chief Justice, as FTL Somalia reported on the opposition accusation . Former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire also accused the President of launching “an assault on the Supreme Court” and deploying troops to its premises, claiming that the Chief Justice and lawyers were “being pursued in their homes for arrest” and that the court’s operations had been halted. His claims could not be independently verified, but images published by Somali media claimed to show military forces in the court’s compound. The presidency has not publicly responded to the Supreme Court’s term-limit ruling, the court’s rejection of the Chief Justice’s dismissal, or the allegations of troop deployment. The Political and Security Context The crisis unfolds against a backdrop of multiple pressures. The United Nations political mission closed a week before the ruling, leaving no agreed mediator for the election dispute. Uganda, the largest contributor to the African Union force, has announced it will withdraw all troops by the end of 2027, and Washington has cut funding for the UN logistics mission that supports the coalition. The opposition has unified behind the court’s ruling. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who brought the challenge, welcomed the judgment and urged the president to negotiate. Former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo had already warned that proceeding without consensus would trigger parallel elections and renewed conflict , and had accused Mohamud of sabotaging internationally mediated talks . As the unravelling of Somalia’s security architecture continues, a political crisis without a clear mechanism for resolution is exactly what analysts warned against. Adnan Abdi Ali, a political analyst at the Somali Center for Studies in Mogadishu, questioned whether the ruling would be enforced at all. “This ruling is unlikely to be implemented, as it comes at a time of ongoing electoral disputes,” he said. Critical Note The Attorney General’s statement is not a legal argument. It is a political declaration dressed in legal language. It accuses the court of procedural violations, but it does not engage with the substance of the ruling: that the President’s mandate expired in May 2026, that the constitutional amendments cannot be applied retroactively to sitting institutions, and that the Chief Justice’s dismissal violated the constitution. The government’s response to the ruling has been consistent: deny its legitimacy, reject its authority, and refuse to engage with its findings. The Attorney General’s office says the ruling “has no legal effect.” But a ruling does not cease to have legal effect because the government says so. It ceases to have effect when a higher authority overturns it, or when the institutions it binds choose to ignore it. There is no higher authority in Somalia’s judicial system than the Supreme Court. The only question now is whether the government will obey the ruling or defy it. The troop deployment around the court, the removal of its Facebook page, and the Attorney General’s rejection of its ruling all point in the same direction. The government is not preparing to comply. It is preparing to govern as if the ruling does not exist. That is a choice with consequences. It means the judiciary has been effectively neutralized as a check on executive power. It means the opposition has no legal venue left to challenge the government’s authority. And it means that the political crisis will not be resolved through law. It will be resolved through whatever means the two sides can bring to bear, and the country will be the poorer for it.
